role: Soldier and officer (team leader) in the Sayeret Matkal special-forces unit; later reservist
description: Enlisted after finishing high school in the United States in 1967 and served five years in Sayeret Matkal, taking part in cross-border raids during the War of Attrition and in the May 1972 rescue of the hijacked Sabena Flight 571, in which he was wounded; Britannica notes that the team was commanded by his later rival Ehud Barak. He remained in the reserves and returned from his studies to fight in the October 1973 Yom Kippur War.
Worked as a consultant at the Boston Consulting Group after his MIT studies, where he was a colleague of Mitt Romney.

organization: Jonathan Netanyahu Anti-Terror Institute (Jonathan Institute), Jerusalem
description: Founded the institute, named after his brother Yonatan, who was killed leading the 1976 Entebbe raid; it organised international conferences on terrorism.
Director of marketing at the Jerusalem company before entering the diplomatic service.

organization: Embassy of Israel in Washington, D.C.
description: Appointed by Ambassador Moshe Arens; during the 1982 Lebanon War he acted as a spokesman for Israel in the US media.

role: Permanent Representative (Ambassador) of Israel to the United Nations
organization: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Israel, New York
description: Ambassador to the United Nations in New York before returning to Israel to run for the Knesset.
Elected on the Likud list in 1988 and re-elected in 1992 and 1996; he resigned his seat after losing the 1999 election for prime minister (Britannica).

Deputy to Foreign Ministers Moshe Arens and David Levy; during the 1991 Gulf War he was a leading spokesman for Israel in international media, and he was a member of the Israeli delegation to the Madrid Conference in 1991.

role: Deputy Minister in the Prime Minister's Office
organization: Government of Israel (Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir)
description: Deputy minister in Yitzhak Shamir's office until Likud lost the 1992 election.

role: Chairman of Likud and Leader of the Opposition
description: Elected Likud leader in March 1993, succeeding Yitzhak Shamir, and led the opposition to the Oslo Accords until 1996; he stepped down as party leader after his 1999 defeat and was succeeded by Ariel Sharon.

Won the first direct election for prime minister in May 1996 and formed a government with ultra-Orthodox and right-wing parties on 18 June 1996, becoming Israel's youngest prime minister. His term saw the Hebron Protocol (1997) and the Wye River Memorandum (1998); several coalition factions quit over Wye, the Knesset voted for early elections and he lost to Ehud Barak in May 1999.
After his 1999 defeat he temporarily left politics and worked for about two years as a consultant to the Israeli communications-equipment maker.
Appointed by Prime Minister Ariel Sharon after the Labor Party left the coalition in 2002; he unsuccessfully challenged Sharon for the Likud leadership the same year.
Returned to the Knesset in the January 2003 election and re-elected in every election since (2006, 2009, 2013, 2015, April and September 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022).

As finance minister during the economic downturn of the Second Intifada he cut public spending and taxes, tied welfare benefits to work or training, privatised state assets including banks, El Al and Zim, and reformed the capital market; supporters credited the programme with the recovery that followed, while Labor critics called it an attack on the social safety net (Wikipedia). He resigned on 7 August 2005 in protest at the Gaza disengagement plan.
Elected Likud leader again in December 2005 after Ariel Sharon left to found Kadima, and re-elected in subsequent leadership contests, including against Gideon Sa'ar in December 2019.
Led the opposition after Likud fell to 12 seats in the March 2006 election, until he formed a government in 2009.

role: Prime Minister of Israel (32nd to 35th governments)
description: Formed a government on 31 March 2009 although Likud finished one seat behind Kadima, and remained prime minister for twelve consecutive years through the elections of 2013, 2015, April and September 2019 and 2020, the last term in a rotation agreement with Benny Gantz. He at times also held other portfolios, including communications minister, the role at issue in Case 4000. The period included the 2014 Gaza war, the 2018 Nation-State Law, the 2020 Abraham Accords and the COVID-19 vaccination campaign. He left office when the Bennett–Lapid government was sworn in on 13 June 2021.
Led the opposition to the Bennett–Lapid government until it lost its majority and the Knesset was dissolved in 2022.

Sworn in on 29 December 2022 at the head of a coalition of Likud, Shas, United Torah Judaism, Religious Zionism, Otzma Yehudit and Noam, described by the Times of Israel as the most hardline government in Israel's history. National Unity joined an emergency government and war cabinet after 7 October 2023 and left in June 2024; United Torah Judaism quit in July 2025. The 37th government became the first since 1973 to complete a full term; the Knesset dispersed on 17 July 2026 and, as of 22 October 2026, the government continues in office pending the 27 October 2026 election and the formation of a new government.
